To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Weyl (dilatation) symmetry is not broken in a conformally invariant theory if one regularises in a Weyl invariant fashion.
Weyl (local conformal) symmetry is not anomalous and the conformal anomaly is a gauge artefact.
the conformal anomaly of a quantum field theory can be amended by a vector field that acts as a dilaton current, and this is the trace of geometric torsion.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question: is conformal symmetry anomalous? We show that if the conformal symmetry is anomalous then it is a consequence of the regularization procedure used, and not a fundamental property of quantum field theory.
the problem of how to quantize conformally invariant theories in a manner that respects the Weyl symmetry and does not generate the conformal anomaly.
the question: is conformal symmetry really broken by quantum effects? We argue that it is not.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
conformal symmetry is not anomalous.
Weyl invariance is not anomalous.
Weyl invariance is an anomaly in the sense of a non-renormalization theorem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Weyl anomaly is not an anomaly at all.
conformal symmetry is not anomalous.
the conformal anomaly does not exist in the usual sense of a violation of conformal symmetry, but is a consequence of regularization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the trace of the torsion tensor is the gauge connection that couples to the dilatation current, which is the only way to amend the conformal anomaly.
Weyl anomalies are artifacts of the regularisation procedure and do not reflect the true quantum behaviour of a theory.
the conformal anomaly is a regularization artifact, which does not exist in the unregularised theory.
